figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic of a symmetric cell geometry for testing separators. Lithium foils are used as anode and cathode, between which are placed one or more separator layers ﬁlled with the electrolyte.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Schematic of a symmetric cell geometry for testing porous-electrode ﬁlms. The active-material ﬁlm is delaminated from its current collector and placed between separators, which in turn are placed between lithium foil electrodes.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Image showing procedure to remove aluminum current collector (curled top layer) from active-material ﬁlm (bottom black layer) using a razor blade.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Nyquist plot obtained from AC impedance experiment for separator cell shown in Fig. 1. The intercept with the real axis at high frequency (R∞) is used to ﬁnd the effective ionic conductivity in the separator region.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 5. Illustration of possible current paths in a cathode ﬁlm. The current ﬂows mostly through the least-resistance path (arrows), making unreliable the measurement of κeff without detailed knowledge of the local behavior of electronic and ionic paths.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Model-experiment comparison for galvanostatic polarization (t < 120 s), fol- lowed by interrupt and relaxation (t > 120 s) in a cell containing three separators.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 7. The variation of the apparent tortuosity τapp with the number of separators. The data suggest good agreement between the AC-impedance and polarization-interrupt experiments. The slope of the linear ﬁt corresponds to the true tortuosity, while the non-zero intercept suggests a surface resistance at the lithium electrodes.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 8. Model-experiment comparison for polarization and relaxation in the LiFePO4 ﬁlm. Two model curves are shown: the ﬁrst is considered the best ﬁt of the relaxation data. The second is shown to illustrate the sensitivity of the model result to tortuosity by using a value that differs from the best ﬁt by 5%.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 9. The effect of porosity on the tortuosity of cathode ﬁlms. The tortuosity is well correlated by a power-law equation (inset).
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 10. TEM image of LiFePO4 particles suggesting a non-monodisperse and non- spherical particle distribution.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf

figures.caption: Fig. 11. Transport model validation from a polarization-interrupt experiment for a thicker LiFePO4 cathode ﬁlm (140 µm) at 45% porosity, where the effective transport properties in the model are parametrized from experiments on thinner (≈100 µm) cells. The good agreement between the model and experiment in terms of relaxation decay rate suggests the tortuosity correlation given in the text is accurate for different thicknesses.
figures.src: 26. Quantifying tortuosity in porous Li-ion battery materials.pdf
